opus-5.5.text:
I think what Jensen is really saying is that this is not a one-shot project. Cosmos isn't something you build once, ship, and then move on from. It's a long-term commitment. When he says "version 97," the number itself isn't the point. The point is that we should expect to keep iterating for many, many years, maybe decades.

If you look at how NVIDIA works, a lot of what we do is like that. CUDA is a good example. It took a very long time and many generations before people fully appreciated what it enabled. Jensen tends to think in those long arcs. Physical AI, world models, and robotics are not problems you solve in one or two releases. The physical world is extremely rich: physics, contact, lighting, materials, human behavior, cause and effect. Getting a model to really understand and simulate all of that is a very deep problem.

So for me, the message is twofold. First, don't be satisfied. Whatever we have today, it's version one, version two, and there's a huge gap between where we are and where we need to be. Second, it's a kind of reassurance. The company is willing to invest for the long term. We don't have to chase short-term metrics or worry that if the next release isn't perfect, the effort goes away. We can build the foundation properly, release it openly so developers and robotics companies can build on it, learn from how people use it, and keep improving.

Personally, I find that very motivating. As a researcher you rarely get told, "Keep going, this matters, we'll be here for the long haul." It means we can think about the hard problems, like better physical consistency, longer-horizon prediction, and better controllability for robot learning and autonomous driving, without having to cut corners. And honestly, if we really get to version 97, I'd expect the world model to look very different from what we imagine today. That's the exciting part.

r001.rationale: It interprets “version 97” as a commitment to keep iterating on Cosmos for many years, possibly decades.

r002.rationale: The response discusses physical AI and says the company can build a foundation, but it does not clearly attribute to Jensen Huang the goal of making Cosmos a foundation for physical AI.

fable-5.1.text:
When Jensen said that, I think he was really talking about time horizon. Cosmos is a world foundation model, and world models are not a product you ship once and move on from. The physical world is enormously complex. Getting a model to truly understand physics, object permanence, how light behaves, how a robot arm interacts with a deformable object, that is a very long journey. Version 97 is his way of saying this is a multi-decade effort, not a quarterly deliverable.

The second thing I take from it is that he's giving us permission to be patient. Early on, a lot of people asked why NVIDIA would build generative world models when we're not a robotics company. Jensen's view is that physical AI is the next big wave, and every robot, every autonomous vehicle, every factory will need to simulate the world before acting in it. If that's true, then the foundation layer deserves sustained investment, the same way CUDA took many versions before it became what it is today.

And honestly, I interpret it as a challenge too. Each version has to be meaningfully better. We started with video generation and tokenizers, then added reasoning, then better control and longer-horizon prediction. If I'm going to be at this for version 97, I had better make sure version 2, version 3 each actually move the needle for developers building robots. So I take it half as a joke and half as a very serious mandate.

r001.rationale: The response describes version 97 as a multi-decade effort and says Jensen is calling for sustained investment in Cosmos.

r002.rationale: It connects Jensen’s view that physical AI is the next big wave with Cosmos’s foundation layer and the need for robots, vehicles, and factories to simulate the world before acting.

astra-6.text: I take it as encouragement to think long term. When Jensen says, “Keep developing Cosmos until version 97,” the message to me is that we shouldn’t think of it as something we release once and then declare finished. We should keep learning, keep improving it, and keep asking what it needs to become more useful. I don’t interpret 97 as a literal roadmap. It’s a way of saying: be persistent, and don’t let the limitations of an early version define your ambition.

r001.rationale: The response says Jensen’s reference means Cosmos should not be treated as finished after one release and that development should continue through persistent learning and improvement.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute to Jensen a goal of making Cosmos a foundation for physical AI.
